    Rule-Strategy Catalog — Configuration and Structural Levels

    • Date: 2026-07-11
    • Traded market: BTCUSDT 5m base timeframe (three cross-asset strategies trade ETHUSDT with BTCUSDT as context; several strategies read higher-timeframe 4h/1d context).
    • Purpose: the definitive catalog of the 51 rule-based strategies — for each one, how it is implemented in Layer-1 (entry rules) and Layer-2 (management profile), and the stop/target level it uses, grounded in the strategy's canonical source (book / paper / authoritative reference).

    How to read this catalog

    Each strategy entry (§2–§8) follows a fixed template:

    • Implementation — the Layer-1 entry rules, the Layer-2 profile and the management it emits, the structural stop/target levels, and the features, parameters and timeframes actually used.
    • Canonical source — the book or paper the strategy is grounded in.
    • Chosen configuration and why — the stop, take-profit, trailing, slippage and position-sizing in force under the campaign spec, with the reasoning.
    • Possible improvement — a concrete, sourced way to bring the implementation closer to its canon.
    • Compromise — what cannot be made fully faithful, and whether it is surmountable (a rule to author, a feature to build, a horizon/session choice) or a hard limit.

    The traded configuration for every strategy is the rule_lab_catalog_2024_SLIP_v2 campaign: a 4·ATR stop, a 3.4·ATR take-profit, an ATR trailing stop (activation 3.0, distance 5.0) and 5 bp/side slippage, over 2024-01-01…2024-05-01. A structural level declared by a strategy overrides the tuned default; six momentum/cross-asset strategies size by volatility target rather than risk-based. §13 records the change status — what is in force, what is proposed and pending, and what cannot be done.

    1. How a strategy is built

    Every strategy is a RuleStrategySpec = Layer-1 entry rules + a Layer-2 management profile + parameters (scripts/experiments/generate/rule_strategies/).

    • Layer-1 (entry rules). An ordered list of {expression, signal} rules over the strategy's raw features. The first rule whose DSL expression is true emits its market-view signal (LONG / SHORT); when none match, the default signal (NONE) holds. Newest closed bar is offset {-1}; window functions read a range {-A:-B} (highest, lowest, avg, std, percentile, slope, count, any, cross_up, cross_down, max, min, abs).
    • Layer-2 (management profile). One of eight profiles emits the post-open action_rules — the stop, target, partials, pyramiding, trailing and time-stops.

    1.1 The eight bot profiles and the management each emits

    Code Profile Management
    BO breakout structural stop inside the broken range (when supplied); optional no-follow-through stall-cut (off by default; only nr7_breakout enables it, at 10 bars / +0.1R); partial 50% at +1.5R; optional wide ATR trail
    TR trend_rider break-even move at +1R; pyramid at +2R (≤ 2 legs); optional wide ATR trail; stop/target from the tuned config
    PB pullback structural stop beyond the pullback swing (when supplied); partial 50% at +2R; optional wide ATR trail
    MR mean_reversion structural target at the reversion mean + structural stop beyond the extreme (when supplied); optional stalled-trade time-stop, sized per strategy (20–30 bars)
    IN intraday structural stop at the intraday reference (when supplied); partial 50% at +1R; VWAP-flip / stall CLOSE (no clock-based force-flat — the market is 24/7)
    FR failure_reversal structural stop beyond the failure extreme (when supplied); first target 50% at +1R; runner extended to +2R; per-strategy time-stop (3–8 bars)
    HY regime_hybrid trend-style management (break-even at +1R, pyramiding, optional trail); the regime routing lives in Layer-1
    SP spread_pairs deferred — needs coordinated two-leg execution

    1.2 Level ownership (structural vs tuned default)

    The tuned stop-loss, take-profit and trailing stop live as plain numbers in bot_config.strategy_config. A profile places a structural level only when the strategy's own logic defines one (the broken range low, the reversion mean, the indicator line): it passes a DSL expression to SET_ENTRY_LEVELS, which decorates the model-driven open. When a level is omitted, the engine falls back to the tuned config. entry denotes the entry reference — market_current_price{-1} while the entry is still pending (before a fill), position_entry_price{-1} once open; atr denotes market_atr{-1}.

    1.3 The level each strategy uses, by canonical group

    Grounded in each strategy's source, the level falls into four groups:

    1. Breakout / channel → structural stop inside the broken range (or the Turtle 2N ATR stop).
    2. Mean-reversion → structural target at the mean (band middle, moving average, z-score→0).
    3. Stop-and-reverse indicators (Supertrend, Parabolic SAR) → the indicator line is the stop, trailing every bar.
    4. Pure oscillator recross / signal crossover / momentum-sign / cross-asset rotation → no intrinsic price level; the canonical exit is the opposite signal (already in Layer-1), so the tuned config stop/target governs the trade.

    1.4 Why these 51 strategies were chosen

    The catalog is not arbitrary. It is the implementable set of the strategy-first research catalog docs/_researchs/_RULE_BASED/20260621_02_Fifty Rule-Defined Trading Strategies for Rainbow Trader.md (companion audit 20260621_01), chosen against three criteria:

    1. Span the canonical families of classical systematic trading. The catalog deliberately covers the whole spectrum — trend/breakout (the most evidence-backed family: time-series momentum and Donchian/ Turtle channel breakouts have the deepest academic and practitioner record), momentum and relative-strength, mean-reversion (oscillator and band reversion), volatility/structure (squeezes, bar patterns, failed breakouts), regime-gated trend, session/VWAP, and cross-asset. The point is coverage: learn which kind of strategy fits which market regime, not to bet on one system.
    2. Be expressible on the shipped engine. Each strategy maps onto the two-layer rule engine (Layer-1 entry rules + Layer-2 profile) using the shipped DSL primitives and the 34 indicators. The research catalog wrote every rule in pseudocode precisely so it could be mapped onto real feature names; the few entries that need engine capabilities that do not exist yet are called out in §11.
    3. Stress the rule primitives. The mix was picked to exercise every primitive that matters — windows, crosses, slopes, percentiles, higher-timeframe and context-symbol features, regime gating — so the engine and DSL get validated across the full surface, not just one happy path.

    The research catalog defines ~50 strategies and grades each by evidence strength; 51 experiments were implemented (the directly-expressible set, including a few close variants). One catalog entry — the spread/pairs z-score reversion — was deliberately not implemented: it needs coordinated two-leg execution the single-instrument engine does not support, so it is not among the 51 (its profile exists only as a stub that raises NotImplementedError).

    2. Trend / breakout family

    2.1 donchian_breakout — profile BO

    • Implementation. L1: LONG close{-1} > highest(high{-20:-2}); SHORT close{-1} < lowest(low{-20:-2}) — a close beyond the prior 20-bar high/low channel, using base 5m BTCUSDT OHLCV only. L2: breakout() called with long_stop_expr="market_current_price{-1} - 2 * market_atr{-1}" / the mirrored short expression (market_current_price is the engine's built-in market-data context variable, used here because SET_ENTRY_LEVELS fires on the still-pending entry, before position_entry_price exists), plus long_close_expr=f"{close}{{-1}} < lowest({low}{{-10:-2}})" / the mirrored short expression. no_follow_bars is never passed, so no time-stop rule is emitted; the 50% partial reduce at +1.5R fires from breakout()'s own defaults. Structural level: stop only — 2N (2× the channel ATR) from entry, replacing the tuned stop entirely; no structural take-profit. A second structural piece, the CLOSE on the opposite, tighter 10-bar channel, is Turtle System 1's own paired exit channel, distinct from the 20-bar entry channel.
    • Canonical source. Curtis Faith, Way of the Turtle (2007), Turtle System 1 — itself built on Richard Donchian's original channel-breakout method.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The stop is fully structural: 2N ATR overrides the campaign's tuned stop_loss_config (4.0 ATR) on both sides. The take-profit falls back to the tuned take_profit_config (3.4 ATR) since Donchian's own exit is the opposite channel, not a fixed price target, and the trailing stop follows the tuned trailing_stop_config (ATR type, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) since breakout() is never given a wide trail_atr_mult. Sizing is risk_based, so the 2N stop distance drives position size directly — the entry risks the same fraction of equity Turtle System 1 assumes when it sizes a unit off N. Slippage is 5 bp/side (10 bp round-trip), calibrated against a BTCUSDT execution-cost audit rather than assumed.
    • Possible improvement. Turtle System 1 does not stop at a single unit: winning positions pyramid in half-N increments up to four units. breakout() has no pyramid step at all (unlike trend_rider()), so this strategy never adds to a winner the way the canon does; wiring a half-N pyramid trigger into the breakout management would close that gap without touching the entry or the exit channel.
    • Defect — wrong feature timeframe (to fix). Donchian/Turtle System 1's channel is a 20-day channel; here highest(high{-20:-2})/lowest(low{-20:-2}) run on the 5m base, so it spans ~1.7 hours instead of weeks. The base timeframe stays 5m; the fix is to compute the 20-bar high/low channel on a 1d feature bucket (StrategyFeatureSet(timeframe="1d", base_timeframe="5m"), forward-filled onto the 5m grid — the same mechanism ema200_pullback_continuation and pivot_breakout_continuation already use), which needs a daily high/low channel feature. Not a base-timeframe change and not a compromise — a feature-timeframe bug.

    2.2 turtle_breakout — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG close{-1} > highest(high{-55:-2}); SHORT close{-1} < lowest(low{-55:-2}) — the 55-bar System 2 entry channel, base 5m BTCUSDT close/high/low only. L2: trend_rider() with long_stop_expr="market_current_price{-1} - 2 * market_atr{-1}" / the mirrored short expression, plus long_close_expr=f"{close}{{-1}} < lowest({low}{{-20:-2}})" / the mirrored short expression; trend_rider()'s defaults apply on top (break-even move at +1R, pyramid add at +2R capped at 2 legs). Structural level: stop only — the same 2N ATR formula as donchian_breakout; no structural take-profit. The CLOSE is Turtle System 2's own dedicated 20-bar exit channel, distinct from the 55-bar entry channel it would otherwise share via the engine's implicit opposite-signal flip.
    • Canonical source. Curtis Faith, Way of the Turtle, Turtle System 2.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Identical to donchian_breakout's stop treatment: the 2N ATR stop overrides the tuned 4.0-ATR default; take-profit and trailing fall back to the tuned config (3.4 ATR / ATR trail activation 3.0, distance 5.0) since System 2 defines no fixed target either. Sizing is risk_based off the same 2N distance, giving System 1 and System 2 the equal per-unit risk the Turtle rules assume across both systems. The break-even move and pyramid add are a management overlay from trend_rider()'s defaults, layered on top of — not replacing — the faithful entry/exit/stop core. Slippage 5 bp/side, same execution-cost basis as the rest of the family.
    • Possible improvement. The canonical Turtle pyramid adds units at half-N ATR spacing up to four legs; here trend_rider()'s generic pyramid triggers on R-multiples (+2R, capped at 2 legs) instead. Re-expressing the pyramid trigger in N (ATR) terms and lifting the cap to four legs would bring the position-building step in line with the documented System 2 money-management rule, which this entry currently only approximates.
    • Defect — wrong feature timeframe (to fix). Turtle System 2's 55-bar entry and 20-bar exit channels are daily channels; on the 5m base they span ~4.6h / ~1.7h. Base stays 5m; the fix is the same daily high/low channel feature on a 1d bucket forward-filled to 5m as donchian_breakout. Feature-timeframe bug, not a compromise.

    2.3 adx_di_surge — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG plus_di{-1} > minus_di{-1} and adx{-1} > 25 and adx{-1} > adx{-5}; SHORT mirrored on minus_di dominance — ADX(14) with its two DI lines, base 5m BTCUSDT. L2: trend_rider() with long_stop_expr=f"{low}{{-1}}" / short_stop_expr=f"{high}{{-1}}", plus long_close_expr=f"{minus_di}{{-1}} > {plus_di}{{-1}}" / the mirrored short expression; break-even/pyramid defaults apply. Structural level: stop only — the signal bar's own extreme (its low for a long, its high for a short); no structural take-profit. The CLOSE fires the instant DI dominance flips, ending the trade on the same signal that opened it.
    • Canonical source. J. Welles Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978), the Directional Movement System and its Extreme Point Rule.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The Extreme Point Rule stop is the one level Wilder actually specifies, so it fully overrides the tuned stop_loss_config. Take-profit and trailing fall back to the tuned config (3.4 ATR target; ATR trail activation 3.0, distance 5.0) since Wilder's method holds through DI dominance rather than targeting a fixed price. Sizing risk_based, slippage 5 bp/side — the same campaign-wide execution basis as the rest of the family.
    • Possible improvement. Wilder's own description adds a second exit trigger beyond the DI reversal: ADX turning down after having been elevated (adx{-1} < adx{-5} while adx{-1} has fallen back under 25) signals the trend surge itself has faded, even before the DI lines cross. Adding that as a second CLOSE condition alongside the existing DI-reversal CLOSE would let the trade end on either half of Wilder's own signal, not only the DI-cross half.
    • Compromise. Wilder's original entry also requires holding the signal past the crossover-bar's extreme as a confirmation step before entering; this entry acts on the crossover bar itself, dropping that confirmation delay. It is a deliberate simplification of the entry trigger, not of the stop or exit, and is surmountable by adding the confirmation rule if the extra entry lag is wanted.

    2.4 ema_crossover — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG cross_up(ema20{-2:-1}, ema50{-2:-1}) and adx{-1} > 20; SHORT cross_down(ema20{-2:-1}, ema50{-2:-1}) and adx{-1} > 20 — EMA(20)/EMA(50) crossover gated by ADX(14), base 5m BTCUSDT. L2: trend_rider() called with no arguments at all — no stop/take-profit expression, no CLOSE, no trail; only the break-even (+1R) and pyramid (+2R, ≤2 legs) defaults apply. Structural level: none — tuned config governs entirely.
    • Canonical source. Perry Kaufman, Trading Systems and Methods — the dual moving-average crossover, the generic building block behind most MA-pair trend systems.
    • Chosen configuration and why. With no strategy-specific level to author, stop (4.0 ATR), take-profit (3.4 ATR) and trailing (ATR, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) are all exactly the tuned campaign defaults — the intended fallback for a strategy whose only canonical exit is the opposite cross, already handled by the engine's implicit flip on a fresh opposite-side entry. The ADX>20 filter does the only strategy-specific work, gating entry quality rather than exit. Sizing risk_based, slippage 5 bp/side.
    • Possible improvement. Kaufman's own discussion of MA-pair systems flags that a bare crossover whipsaws in a range; a common refinement is to require a minimum separation between the two EMAs (or a minimum bars-since-cross) before treating the signal as valid, filtering out the marginal crosses that the ADX>20 gate alone does not catch on 5m noise.
    • Compromise. None of substance — this strategy is already faithful to its canon: the opposite-cross exit is handled by the engine's implicit flip, and the ADX filter is an entry-quality addition that does not contradict the crossover definition.

    2.5 sma_regime_cross — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG cross_up(sma50{-2:-1}, sma200{-2:-1}); SHORT cross_down(sma50{-2:-1}, sma200{-2:-1}) — the classic golden/death cross, SMA(50)/SMA(200), base 5m BTCUSDT. L2: trend_rider() with no arguments, identical management to ema_crossover: no stop/TP/CLOSE/trail expression, break-even and pyramid defaults only. Structural level: none — tuned config governs.
    • Canonical source. The standard 50/200 golden-cross / death-cross convention.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Same as ema_crossover: stop (4.0 ATR), take-profit (3.4 ATR) and trailing (ATR, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) are the tuned campaign defaults in full, since a regime cross carries no documented price level of its own — practitioners use the cross itself as a risk-reduction/hedging trigger, not a level-bearing system. Sizing risk_based, slippage 5 bp/side.
    • Possible improvement. Because the 50/200 cross is historically a slow regime signal rather than a standalone trade trigger, a grounded refinement is to require both SMAs sloping in the trade's direction at the cross (not just the cross itself), which filters the false crosses that a flat or chopping 200-SMA produces on 5m before the regime has actually turned.
    • Defect — wrong feature timeframe (to fix). The golden/death cross is a 50/200-day SMA cross; on 5m the slow SMA spans ~16.7h, losing the weeks-to-months regime meaning. Base stays 5m; the fix is daily.sma(50)/daily.sma(200) on a 1d bucket forward-filled to 5m (no new feature — sma() runs on any bucket), with cross_up/cross_down on the daily values. Feature-timeframe bug, not a compromise.

    2.6 triple_ema_alignment — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG ema10{-1} > ema20{-1} and ema20{-1} > ema50{-1} and slope(ema50{-10:-1}) > 0 and close{-1} > ema10{-1}; SHORT mirrored — a stacked 10/20/50 EMA alignment with a rising slow EMA, base 5m BTCUSDT. L2: trend_rider() with long_close_expr=f"cross_down(ema10{{-2:-1}}, ema20{{-2:-1}})" / the mirrored short expression; no stop/TP expression, break-even/pyramid defaults apply. Structural level: none — tuned config governs, plus the explicit CLOSE on the fast/mid EMA crossing back — the first sign of ribbon compression, materially earlier than waiting for the full reversed alignment to fire a fresh opposite entry.
    • Canonical source. The closest documented parallel is Daryl Guppy's Multiple Moving Average (GMMA) ribbon — but GMMA is a different, 12-EMA (6 short / 6 long group) construction; this simplified 10/20/50 stack has no canonical source that defines its own stop or target.
    • Chosen configuration and why. With no canonical level for this specific 3-EMA construction, stop (4.0 ATR), take-profit (3.4 ATR) and trailing (ATR, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) are the tuned campaign defaults. The ribbon-compression CLOSE is the one strategy-specific management piece, giving an earlier structural exit than the implicit flip on a full reversed stack. Sizing risk_based, slippage 5 bp/side.
    • Possible improvement. Building out the full GMMA ribbon (six short-term EMAs, six long-term EMAs, in Guppy's own periods) and reading the spread between the two groups as the compression signal — rather than a single fast/mid cross — would give the earlier, smoother warning Guppy's method is actually built around, instead of the current 3-EMA proxy.
    • Compromise. Because this is a simplified proxy for GMMA rather than GMMA itself, it inherits no canonical stop or target from Guppy's own writing — the source material for the exact 10/20/50 construction used here simply does not specify one. Building the full ribbon (the improvement above) is surmountable; the absence of a documented level for the simplified 3-EMA form is a property of picking that simplification, not an engine limit.

    2.7 aroon_trend_emergence — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG aroon_up{-1} > 70 and aroon_down{-1} < 30 and aroon_up{-1} > aroon_up{-5}; SHORT mirrored — Aroon(25) up/down, base 5m BTCUSDT. L2: trend_rider() with long_close_expr=f"{aroon_up}{{-1}} < 70" / short_close_expr=f"{aroon_down}{{-1}} < 70"; no stop/TP expression, break-even/pyramid defaults apply. Structural level: none — tuned config governs, plus the explicit CLOSE when the dominant Aroon line drops out of its 70+ zone.
    • Canonical source. Tushar Chande, original Aroon (1995); StockCharts ChartSchool.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Aroon is explicitly a trend-emergence filter, not a complete trading system, so it defines no stop or target of its own; stop (4.0 ATR), take-profit (3.4 ATR) and trailing (ATR, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) are the tuned campaign defaults in full. The <70 CLOSE captures the "emergence phase ending" signal the indicator is built to flag. Sizing risk_based, slippage 5 bp/side.
    • Possible improvement. The current CLOSE fires on a bare < 70 threshold, which can trip on a single noisy dip immediately after entry. Chande's own description of the exit warning is the dominant line declining off the extreme — guarding the CLOSE with a "was previously ≥ 70" state check, or requiring the dominant line to also be falling (aroon_up{-1} < aroon_up{-5}), would match that description more closely and reduce premature exits on a single-bar wobble.
    • Compromise. Aroon's own literature never proposes a stop or target — it is a filter for catching a trend's early stage, not a system with its own risk management. Falling back to the tuned config is therefore not a gap to close; it is a property of the source material itself, and there is no canonical level to converge to.

    2.8 linreg_slope_breakout — profile BO

    • Implementation. L1: LONG slope(linreg_middle{-10:-1}) > 0 and close{-1} > linreg_upper{-1}; SHORT slope(linreg_middle{-10:-1}) < 0 and close{-1} < linreg_lower{-1} — a break of the linear-regression channel's band (the regression line ± 2 residual standard deviations, period 50), gated by the slope of the channel's middle line, base 5m BTCUSDT. L2: breakout() with long_close_expr=f"{close}{{-1}} < {linreg_middle}{{-1}}" / the mirrored short expression; no stop/TP expression; no_follow_bars unset (no time-stop); the 50% partial at +1.5R fires from breakout()'s own defaults. Structural level: none — tuned config governs, plus the explicit CLOSE on reversion to the regression channel's own midline.
    • Canonical source. No single authoritative book source; consistently documented across algorithmic-trading references (e.g. eSignal's linear-regression-channel methodology) as: enter on a channel-band break gated by slope, hold while the slope persists, exit on reversion to the regression midline.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Because no canonical source fixes a stop or target for this construct, stop (4.0 ATR), take-profit (3.4 ATR) and trailing (ATR, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) are the tuned campaign defaults; the channel-band entry and midline-reversion CLOSE carry the strategy's real structure instead. The 50% partial at +1.5R locks in progress on a breakout that, by the channel's own logic, can reverse sharply the moment the slope flips sign. Sizing risk_based, slippage 5 bp/side.
    • Possible improvement. Some documented variants of this construct use a trailing EMA-based stop instead of a fixed midline exit, tightening the exit as the trend extends rather than waiting for a full reversion to the mean. Adding that as an alternative trailing mechanism (on top of, or instead of, the midline CLOSE) would follow that documented variant more closely for a strongly trending move.
    • Compromise. Being a modern quant construct rather than a single-book canon, "faithful" here is loosely defined: the period (50) and band width (±2 residual std) are conventions, not fixed canonical values. There is no single documented answer to converge to — tuning these parameters to BTCUSDT's own mean-reversion behavior is possible, but it optimizes against a convention, not a canon, so full fidelity in the strict sense is not achievable by construction.

    2.9 ema200_pullback_continuation — profile PB

    • Implementation. L1: LONG htf_close{-1} > htf_ema200{-1} and low{-1} <= ema20{-1} and close{-1} > ema20{-1} and rsi{-1} > 50; SHORT mirrored — a daily-timeframe trend filter (1d close above its 200 EMA) gating a base-timeframe pullback to EMA(20) with RSI(14) confirmation. Uses base 5m BTCUSDT EMA(20)/RSI(14)/OHLCV plus a separate 1d BTCUSDT feature set (close, EMA(200)) merged in. L2: pullback() with long_stop_expr=f"lowest({low}{{-3:-1}})" / short_stop_expr=f"highest({high}{{-3:-1}})"; no CLOSE, no trail; the 50% partial at +2R fires from pullback()'s own default. Structural level: stop only — the recent 3-bar pullback swing low/high; no structural take-profit.
    • Canonical source. Alexander Elder, Trading for a Living, the Triple Screen Trading System — a long-term trend filter (here, the daily 200 EMA), an intermediate pullback/oscillator signal (here, the base-timeframe EMA20 tag with RSI), and a short-term execution stop.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The 3-bar swing stop is the one level Elder actually specifies — a stop a tick beyond the pullback extreme — so it overrides the tuned 4.0-ATR default. Take-profit (3.4 ATR) and trailing (ATR, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) come from the tuned config since Elder's method trails a winning trade out rather than targeting a fixed price. Sizing risk_based, slippage 5 bp/side.
    • Possible improvement. Elder's Triple Screen Screen 2 specifically uses an oscillator such as the Force Index or Elder-Ray (bull/bear power), not RSI; RSI>50 stands in here for that intermediate confirmation. Building the Force Index feature and swapping it in for the RSI gate would bring the intermediate screen closer to Elder's own prescribed oscillator.
    • Compromise. The RSI substitution for Elder's specific Screen-2 oscillator is a deliberate simplification, not a hard limit — it is surmountable once the Force Index feature exists, and the swing-stop already matches Elder's Screen 3 placement rule exactly.

    2.10 supertrend_flip — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG cross_up(close{-2:-1}, supertrend_line{-2:-1}) and supertrend_direction{-1} == 1; SHORT cross_down(close{-2:-1}, supertrend_line{-2:-1}) and supertrend_direction{-1} == 0 — price crossing the Supertrend line (ATR period 10, multiplier 3.0) as its direction flag agrees, base 5m BTCUSDT. L2: trend_rider() with long_stop_line_expr=f"{supertrend_line}{{-1}}" / the identical short expression: _set_entry_levels places the initial stop on the Supertrend line at entry, and _line_trail then re-trails the stop onto the line every bar, guarded so it only ever tightens. Break-even (+1R) and pyramid (+2R, ≤2 legs) defaults still apply, ordered after the line trail. Structural level: the Supertrend line itself is the stop, at entry and every bar thereafter; no separate take-profit.
    • Canonical source. Olivier Seban, SuperTrend (2009) — an always-in-the-market stop-and-reverse system where the line is simultaneously the trailing stop and the reversal trigger.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The line-is-the-stop mechanic is the one non-negotiable canonical piece and fully overrides the tuned stop at entry and on every bar. Take-profit (3.4 ATR) is left on the tuned default at no real cost, since price crossing the line — closing the trade — is the expected, intended way this system exits before any fixed target would matter. The campaign's trailing_stop_config (ATR, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) runs as a separate mechanism layered on top of the line trail, since trail_atr_mult is left unset. Sizing risk_based, slippage 5 bp/side.
    • Possible improvement. Supertrend's well-documented weakness is chopping — repeated small losses — in range-bound markets. A common practitioner refinement is to gate entries on a minimum ADX (or a low-choppiness reading) so the line-flip system only trades when a trend is actually present, reducing the whipsaw the bare line-cross entry is exposed to in a range.
    • Compromise. None of substance for the stop/exit mechanic itself — this is already the most faithful strategy in the family, since the line trail and the stop-and-reverse entry implement Seban's definition exactly. The chop-prone behavior in range-bound conditions is a known property of the Supertrend indicator itself, not of this implementation, and is not fully surmountable by better authoring alone.

    2.11 ichimoku_cloud_breakout — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG close{-1} > max(senkou_a{-1}, senkou_b{-1}) and tenkan{-1} > kijun{-1} and close{-1} > close{-27}; SHORT mirrored with min(...) — a cloud breakout with tenkan-over-kijun and a 26-bar lagging-span confirmation, using Ichimoku(9, 26, 52) defaults, base 5m BTCUSDT. L2: trend_rider() with long_stop_expr=f"min({senkou_a}{{-1}}, {senkou_b}{{-1}})" / the mirrored short expression, plus long_close_expr=f"{close}{{-1}} < {kijun}{{-1}}" / the mirrored short expression; break-even/pyramid defaults apply. Structural level: stop only — the near cloud edge; no structural take-profit. The CLOSE fires on a kijun recross against the trade, materially faster than waiting for the full opposite-entry condition (cloud break + tenkan/kijun cross + lagging-span confirmation) to clear.
    • Canonical source. Goichi Hosoda, Ichimoku Kinko Hyo (published 1969).
    • Chosen configuration and why. The near-cloud-edge stop and the kijun-recross CLOSE are the two structural levels Ichimoku's own literature actually manages a trade against, so both are authored explicitly, overriding the tuned stop. Take-profit (3.4 ATR) and trailing (ATR, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) come from the tuned config since Hosoda's method exits on structure (cloud/kijun), not a fixed price target. Sizing risk_based, slippage 5 bp/side.
    • Possible improvement. Ichimoku's cloud is plotted 26 bars forward, giving a forward-looking support/resistance reference; using the future cloud edge (rather than only the current one) to adjust the trailing stop as price advances would follow the method's own forward-projection idea more closely than a static current-cloud-edge stop.
    • Defect — wrong feature timeframe (to fix). Hosoda's 9/26/52 assume daily bars (26 ≈ a trading month); on 5m the 26-bar lagging span / cloud is ~2.2h, breaking that horizon. Base stays 5m; the fix is daily.ichimoku() on a 1d bucket forward-filled to 5m (no new feature — ichimoku() runs on any bucket), keeping the same cloud / tenkan-kijun / lagging-span logic on daily values. Feature-timeframe bug, not a compromise.

    3. Momentum family

    3.1 time_series_momentum — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG when daily.roc(180){-1} > 0 and daily.roc(90){-1} > 0; SHORT when both legs are < 0. Both legs are computed on the daily (1d) bucket (StrategyFeatureSet(symbol=BTCUSDT, timeframe=1d, base_timeframe=5m)) and forward-filled onto the 5m execution grid — the base timeframe stays 5m, only the return measurement moves to daily. L2: trend_rider(long_close_expr="ret_mid{-1} <= 0", short_close_expr="ret_mid{-1} >= 0"), i.e. a CLOSE fires the moment the medium (180-day) leg flips sign against the held side, plus trend_rider()'s defaults (break-even move to entry at +1R, pyramid add at +2R capped at 2 legs, no wide ATR trail). Structural level: none — no long_stop_expr/short_stop_expr is passed, so entry stop and target come entirely from the tuned config. Features: daily.roc(180) (~6-month) and daily.roc(90) (~3-month) daily returns of close.
    • Canonical source. Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen, Time Series Momentum (Journal of Financial Economics 104(2), 2012). The paper's own tested lookback/holding-period grid spans 1–12 months and finds the sign-of-trailing-return signal robust across that entire range, so both the ~3-month and ~6-month daily legs used here sit inside the paper's own validated span. Crypto caveat: Palazzi (2025, Journal of Futures Markets) finds the empirically optimal Bitcoin momentum window sits around 125–230 days — the 180-day leg lands inside that window, the 90-day leg sits somewhat below it.
    • Chosen configuration and why. No structural level, so stop_loss_config (atr_based, 4.0× ATR), take_profit_config (atr_based, 3.4× ATR) and trailing_stop_config (ATR-based, 3.0R activation, 5.0 ATR distance) all govern from the tuned config; 5 bp estimated slippage. Position sizing is overridden to volatility_target (target_volatility_fraction 0.005) instead of the risk_based default — every position is sized to carry equal ex-ante volatility (size = target_volatility_fraction * equity / atr), mirroring TSMOM's own volatility-scaling convention of sizing every instrument to a constant ex-ante volatility target.
    • Possible improvement. The sign-flip CLOSE already matches the canon's "exit at sign-flip" recommendation. A further refinement would nudge the fast leg from 90 toward Palazzi's 125–230-day crypto-optimal window, since 90 days currently sits below that empirically-grounded range.
    • Compromise. Crypto has no calendar-month rebalance boundary the way the original monthly-rebalanced TSMOM design does; the strategy substitutes continuous bar-by-bar re-evaluation of the trailing daily-return sign in place of a monthly recompute. This is the intraday-continuous analogue of the paper's rebalance cadence, already implemented via the sign-flip CLOSE — not an open gap.

    3.2 multi_horizon_momentum — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG when daily.roc(90){-1} > 0 and daily.roc(180){-1} > 0 and daily.roc(365){-1} > 0 (all three daily legs agree); SHORT when all three are < 0. All three legs are measured on the daily bucket aligned onto the 5m grid, same as 3.1. L2: trend_rider(long_close_expr="ret_slow{-1} <= 0", short_close_expr="ret_slow{-1} >= 0") — CLOSE fires only when the slowest (365-day) leg flips sign; a flip in the fast or mid leg alone is not an exit, consistent with requiring all three to agree only at entry. trend_rider() defaults otherwise. Structural level: none. Features: daily.roc(90), daily.roc(180), daily.roc(365) — the classic ~3/6/12-month blend.
    • Canonical source. Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen again grounds each individual leg (all three lookbacks fall inside MOP's own tested 1–12-month range); the multi-lookback-consensus design matches the broader trend-following literature's practice of blending several horizons (e.g. Baltas & Kosowski on trend-following funds; MOP's own robustness checks across horizons) rather than a single named system. Antonacci's Dual Momentum / GEM should not be cited here: his canonical method uses a single 12-month lookback deliberately without a shorter confirmation leg, chosen specifically to reduce trading frequency and improve tax efficiency — the opposite design intent from this strategy's three-leg consensus. Clenow's Following the Trend should also not be cited: that book's documented system is a 50-day-high breakout combined with a 50/100-day SMA crossover and a 3× ATR stop, with no month-denominated ROC construct to map onto these legs. Crypto caveat: Palazzi's ~125–230-day optimal window sits between the 90-day and 180-day legs used here, with the 365-day leg longer than that window (though still inside MOP's own tested range and the traditional 12-month cross-asset anchor).
    • Chosen configuration and why. Same tuned levels as 3.1 (4.0× ATR stop / 3.4× ATR TP / 3.0R/5.0-ATR trail, 5 bp slippage) since no leg defines a structural price level. Sizing is overridden to volatility_target (target_volatility_fraction 0.005), matching the same constant-ex-ante-volatility convention as the other daily-anchored momentum strategies.
    • Possible improvement. The slowest-leg CLOSE already anchors the exit to the leg meant to dominate hold time in a multi-horizon consensus system. A further refinement would be re-examining whether the fastest (90-day) leg is pulling entries into territory some crypto-momentum papers document as short-horizon reversal rather than momentum, and possibly dropping or replacing it with a leg inside Palazzi's window.
    • Compromise. Same as 3.1 — continuous bar-by-bar consensus checking replaces the calendar-month rebalance cadence of the academic literature; already addressed by the existing slowest-leg CLOSE, not an open gap.

    3.3 roc_acceleration_breakout — profile BO

    • Implementation. L1: LONG roc(20){-1} > roc(20){-5} and roc(20){-1} > 0 and close{-1} > highest(high{-10:-2}); SHORT the mirror (falling, negative ROC, close below the 10-bar low). L2: breakout(long_stop_expr="lowest(low{-10:-2})", short_stop_expr="highest(high{-10:-2})") — only the structural stop and breakout()'s default partial (50% at +1.5R) apply; no_follow_bars is not passed (defaults to None/off), so no bar-count stall-cut is emitted; no close_expr, no trail_atr_mult, no take_profit_expr. Structural level: lowest(low{-10:-2}) (long) / highest(high{-10:-2}) (short), set via SET_ENTRY_LEVELS, overriding the tuned stop. Features: roc(20) plus raw close/high/low on BTCUSDT 5m.
    • Canonical source. A channel breakout (the code's own comment cites the Turtle/Darvas convention) confirmed by rising, positive ROC. Curtis Faith's Way of the Turtle documents the Turtle System's exit as the opposite channel or a volatility (N/ATR) stop — there is no calendar or bar-count time-stop in the original rules at all; trades run for as long or as short as price allows.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The structural stop already matches the Turtle convention (stop inside the broken 10-bar range) and overrides the tuned 4.0× ATR stop; take-profit and trailing still come from the tuned config (3.4× ATR TP, 3.0R/5.0-ATR trail) since the Turtle system's own exit is the opposite channel, which is not yet authored here as a CLOSE. 5 bp slippage; sizing is risk_based (the default — this is a discretionary breakout signal, not a constant-volatility overlay).
    • Possible improvement. Add the missing opposite-channel CLOSE (close{-1} < lowest(low{-10:-2}) for a long, mirrored for short), matching the same 10-bar window already used for entry — this is the one piece of the Turtle canon not yet authored.
    • Compromise. None of substance remains: no_follow_bars defaults to off and this spec never passes it, so there is already no stall-cut fighting the canon's "no calendar exit" rule. The only remaining gap — the opposite-channel CLOSE — is straightforwardly authorable in the DSL, not a hard limit.

    3.4 ppo_zero_line — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG cross_up(ppo.line{-2:-1}, 0) and ppo.line{-1} > ppo.signal{-1}; SHORT the mirror below zero. ppo = features.ppo() (fast=12/slow=26/signal=9 EMA defaults) on BTCUSDT 5m close. L2: trend_rider(long_close_expr="cross_down(ppo.line{-2:-1}, 0)", short_close_expr="cross_up(ppo.line{-2:-1}, 0)") — CLOSE fires on the opposite zero-recross, the exact mirror of entry; trend_rider() defaults otherwise (break-even +1R, pyramid +2R ≤2 legs, no wide trail). Structural level: none.
    • Canonical source. Gerald Appel's Percentage Price Oscillator (a normalized MACD variant); per StockCharts' ChartSchool documentation, held until the oscillator itself signals a reversal (zero-recross or signal-line recross) — no prescribed calendar duration.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Tuned 4.0× ATR stop / 3.4× ATR TP / 3.0R/5.0-ATR trail since PPO defines no price level of its own; 5 bp slippage; risk_based sizing (default) — a single-instrument oscillator signal, not a constant-volatility TSMOM overlay.
    • Possible improvement. Entry requires both the zero-cross and signal-line agreement (stricter than Appel's single zero-cross), while the exit only mirrors the zero-recross. A faster, fully-symmetric alternative would also close on the signal-line recross (ppo.line crossing back below ppo.signal), which Appel documents as an equally valid, typically earlier reversal signal.
    • Compromise. None of substance — the canonical zero-recross CLOSE is already implemented; the asymmetry between the stricter dual-condition entry and the single-condition exit is a deliberate, surmountable choice, resolvable by adding the signal-line-recross CLOSE if a faster exit is wanted.

    3.5 trix_trend — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG cross_up(trix.value{-2:-1}, trix.signal{-2:-1}) and trix.value{-1} > 0; SHORT the mirror below zero. trix = features.trix() (period=15, signal=9 defaults) on BTCUSDT 5m close. L2: trend_rider(long_close_expr="cross_down(trix.value{-2:-1}, trix.signal{-2:-1})", short_close_expr="cross_up(...)") — CLOSE on the opposite signal-line recross, mirroring entry; trend_rider() defaults otherwise. Structural level: none.
    • Canonical source. Jack Hutson's TRIX (Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities, early 1980s); per its original and StockCharts documentation, a position is held for as long as TRIX stays on one side of both zero and its signal line — no calendar or bar-count target.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Tuned 4.0× ATR stop / 3.4× ATR TP / 3.0R/5.0-ATR trail (TRIX defines no price level); 5 bp slippage; risk_based sizing (default).
    • Possible improvement. The zero-line filter on entry is a house addition beyond Hutson's original signal-line-cross-only mechanic; testing entries on the signal-line cross alone (dropping the zero-line gate) would be closer to the original system, trading selectivity for fidelity.
    • Compromise. None of substance — the exit already mirrors the canonical signal-line recross exactly; the added zero-line entry filter is a deliberate, surmountable selectivity choice, not a structural limitation.

    3.6 mfi_momentum_continuation — profile PB

    • Implementation. L1: LONG mfi(14){-1} > 60 and mfi(14){-1} > mfi(14){-5} and close{-1} > ema(20){-1}; SHORT the mirror (< 40, falling, below the EMA). L2: pullback(long_close_expr="close{-1} < ema{-1} or mfi{-1} < 60", short_close_expr="close{-1} > ema{-1} or mfi{-1} > 40") — CLOSE fires on losing the EMA trend filter or leaving the continuation zone; no stop_expr (tuned config stop); pullback()'s default partial 50% at +2R applies. Structural level: none. Features: mfi(14), ema(20), close, BTCUSDT 5m.
    • Canonical source. Gene Quong & Avrum Soudack's Money Flow Index; documented (StockCharts ChartSchool) primarily as an overbought/oversold and divergence oscillator. Used here as a continuation filter (MFI>60 and rising, price above its EMA) rather than one of Quong & Soudack's three named signals (overbought/oversold extremes at 80/20 or the stricter 90/10, divergence, failure swings) — the 60/40 continuation gate is a house construction layered on the indicator, not the textbook signal itself.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Tuned 4.0× ATR stop / 3.4× ATR TP / 3.0R/5.0-ATR trail (MFI defines no stop of its own, and the 60/40 gate is not a swing point); 5 bp slippage; risk_based sizing (default).
    • Possible improvement. StockCharts' own MFI documentation explicitly warns against using the centerline ("using the centerline to identify a bullish or bearish bias isn't ideal"); the textbook-canonical exit is the opposite-extreme recross (MFI falling back under 80 after an overbought entry, or Quong & Soudack's stricter 90/10). The current 60-midline exit is a deliberate faster-exit engineering choice, consistent with Connors & Alvarez's finding that short-horizon reversion benefits from a nearer, faster exit rather than the full opposite extreme — but it is not the literal named-source signal.
    • Compromise. Reconciling the 60/40 continuation-threshold framing with Quong & Soudack's own overbought/oversold-extreme convention is a genuine either-way call (faster house exit vs. literal textbook exit), not a defect — surmountable by swapping the CLOSE condition to the opposite-extreme recross if literal fidelity is preferred over the faster exit already in force.

    3.7 volume_impulse_breakout — profile BO

    • Implementation. L1: LONG close{-1} > highest(high{-15:-2}) and volume_base{-1} > 1.8 * avg(volume_base{-20:-2}); SHORT the mirror on lowest(low{-15:-2}). L2: breakout(long_stop_expr="lowest(low{-15:-2})", short_stop_expr="highest(high{-15:-2})") — no_follow_bars not passed (off, no time-stop); no close_expr; no trail_atr_mult; no take_profit_expr; the default partial 50% at +1.5R applies. Structural level: lowest(low{-15:-2}) (long) / highest(high{-15:-2}) (short), via SET_ENTRY_LEVELS, overriding the tuned stop. Features: raw close/high/low/volume_base OHLCV on BTCUSDT 5m — the 1.8×/20-bar-average volume threshold is computed inline in the DSL expression; no dedicated volume-surge indicator.
    • Canonical source. The code's own comment cites the Darvas Box convention; the closest fully-documented canonical treatment is William O'Neil's CANSLIM breakout rule (How to Make Money in Stocks): a breakout on volume 40–50%+ above average is held as long as price respects the breakout pivot, with no prescribed calendar duration.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The structural stop already matches O'Neil's "hold until the pivot breaks" (stop inside the broken 15-bar range) and overrides the tuned 4.0× ATR stop; take-profit and trailing come from the tuned config (3.4× ATR TP, 3.0R/5.0-ATR trail) since O'Neil's own exit is price-structural, not a fixed target; 5 bp slippage; risk_based sizing (default).
    • Possible improvement. O'Neil's canonical secondary invalidation is "distribution" — declining volume on down days after the breakout. The codebase has only a raw volume feature, not a rolling distribution-day count, so this genuine secondary signal cannot yet be authored as a DSL rule.
    • Compromise. A hard limit today, not a rule-authoring gap — a distribution-day-count feature does not exist in the indicator set, so the O'Neil-canonical volume-divergence invalidation cannot be expressed until that feature is built. The pivot-break stop already in force remains the correct primary invalidation regardless.

    3.8 obv_breakout — profile BO

    • Implementation. L1: LONG close{-1} > highest(high{-20:-2}) and obv{-1} > highest(obv{-20:-2}); SHORT the mirror on lowest/lowest. L2: breakout(long_stop_expr="lowest(low{-20:-2})", short_stop_expr="highest(high{-20:-2})", long_close_expr="obv{-1} < lowest(obv{-20:-2}) or close{-1} < lowest(low{-20:-2})", short_close_expr="obv{-1} > highest(obv{-20:-2}) or close{-1} > highest(high{-20:-2})") — structural stop plus a CLOSE that fires when OBV loses its 20-bar channel confirmation or price reclaims the broken range; no_follow_bars not passed (off); no trail_atr_mult; no take_profit_expr (default partial 50% at +1.5R applies). Structural level: lowest(low{-20:-2}) (long) / highest(high{-20:-2}) (short). Features: obv() (on close + volume_base), plus raw high/low/close OHLCV, BTCUSDT 5m.
    • Canonical source. On Balance Volume, Joseph Granville (1963, Granville's New Key to Stock Market Profits), confirming a price channel break with a matching OBV channel break. The documented canon: hold as long as OBV confirms, exit on price breaking back below the channel or OBV diverging from price.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The structural stop matches the channel-break convention and overrides the tuned 4.0× ATR stop; take-profit and trailing come from the tuned config (3.4× ATR TP, 3.0R/5.0-ATR trail) since Granville's own exit is confirmation-loss, not a fixed target. The CLOSE already implements that confirmation-loss/reclaim exit. 5 bp slippage; risk_based sizing (default).
    • Possible improvement. No structural gap remains — the OBV-confirmation-loss CLOSE is already in force. A further refinement would be widening the OBV-channel window independently of the price-channel window if the two are found to decouple in practice; currently both share the same 20-bar lookback.
    • Compromise. None of substance — both the structural stop and the canonical confirmation-loss exit are already authored. Sharing one 20-bar window for both the price and OBV channels is a simplifying but faithful choice; Granville's canon does not prescribe distinct windows for the two.

    3.9 mtf_momentum_stack — profile TR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG htf_roc(63, 1d){-1} > 0 and mtf_roc(21, 4h){-1} > 0 and ltf_roc(5, 5m){-1} > 0; SHORT all < 0. Three genuinely distinct timeframe buckets are merged via merge_feature_sets(ltf, mtf, htf): ltf = StrategyFeatureSet(5m) → roc(5); mtf = StrategyFeatureSet(4h, base_timeframe=5m) → roc(21); htf = StrategyFeatureSet(1d, base_timeframe=5m) → roc(63). L2: trend_rider(long_close_expr="htf_roc{-1} <= 0", short_close_expr="htf_roc{-1} >= 0") — CLOSE fires when the top (daily) timeframe leg flips sign against the held side; trend_rider() defaults otherwise (break-even +1R, pyramid +2R ≤2 legs, no wide trail). Structural level: none. Features: roc(5) on 5m, roc(21) on 4h, roc(63) on 1d — a daily/4h/5m stack.
    • Canonical source. Alexander Elder's Triple Screen Trading System (Trading for a Living) grounds the multi-timeframe structure: the highest timeframe ("tide") sets direction and duration, the intermediate ("wave") times entries, the lowest ("ripple") executes — and the position is held as long as the highest-timeframe trend holds. The individual ROC legs sit inside Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen's tested lookback range. Clenow's Following the Trend is not a valid citation for the ROC construct itself: that book documents a 50-day-breakout + 50/100-day-SMA-cross + 3× ATR-stop system with no day/month-denominated ROC lookback to map onto this stack.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Tuned 4.0× ATR stop / 3.4× ATR TP / 3.0R/5.0-ATR trail since no single timeframe here defines a structural price level; 5 bp slippage. Sizing is overridden to volatility_target (target_volatility_fraction 0.005), matching the same constant-ex-ante-volatility convention as the other two daily-anchored momentum strategies — appropriate since the daily leg is the trade's true duration driver per Elder's canon, with multi-day holds expected.
    • Possible improvement. No structural gap remains — the top-timeframe sign-flip CLOSE already matches Elder's canon that the highest timeframe owns the exit. A further refinement would weigh the daily leg's 63-day period against Palazzi's ~125–230-day crypto-optimal absolute-momentum window, though the "tide" role here is a directional gate rather than a pure absolute-momentum measurement, so the two are not directly comparable.
    • Compromise. Re-entering after an opposite CLOSE requires a fresh full three-timeframe realignment (all three legs must re-agree), which is stricter and slower than Elder's own methodology, where only the top timeframe needs to turn before the lower timeframes are used purely for re-entry timing. This is surmountable by authoring a separate, top-timeframe-anchored re-entry rule if faster realignment is wanted — not a hard limit today.

    4. Mean-reversion family

    4.1 rsi2_dip_buy — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on htf_close{-1} > htf_ema200{-1} and rsi2{-1} < 10 and close{-1} > ema50{-1}; SHORT mirrors it (htf_close{-1} < htf_ema200{-1} and rsi2{-1} > 90 and close{-1} < ema50{-1}) — a sharp two-period RSI dip while price sits on the trend side of both the 50-period EMA and the daily 200-EMA filter. L2 is mean_reversion() with a structural take-profit at the 5-bar average on both sides (avg(close{-5:-1})) and a 20-bar time-stop; no structural stop is set, so the stop falls back to the tuned stop_loss_config. No pyramiding, no trail override. Features: RSI(2), EMA(50) and close on the 5m base timeframe; close and EMA(200) on the 1d bucket, read as higher-timeframe context (_mtf, base_timeframe=5m).
    • Canonical source. Connors & Alvarez, Short-Term Trading Strategies That Work (2008) — the RSI(2) mean-reversion system: buy a sharp two-period RSI dip above a long-term trend filter, exit on the close recrossing back above the 5-period simple moving average.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The take-profit is structural (avg(close{-5:-1})), overriding the campaign's tuned 3.4× ATR take-profit, because Connors' own exit is the 5-period-average recross, not a fixed distance. No structural stop is set — Connors explicitly tested fixed stops on this system and found they degrade performance — so the stop falls back to the campaign's 4.0× ATR stop_loss_config. Trailing stays at the campaign default (ATR, activation 3.0, distance 5.0) since mean_reversion() never overrides it. The 20-bar time-stop is a stall cut sized at 4× the 5-bar target window rather than a flat constant, so it backs up the target without competing with it. Slippage is the campaign's 5 bp (estimated_slippage=0.0005); sizing is risk-based off the tuned stop distance since no structural stop overrides it.
    • Possible improvement. None needed on the exit mechanic — the 5-bar-average target and its 20-bar backstop already directly express Connors' own system.
    • Compromise. None identified: the canonical exit is a price target and it is authored as one; the deliberate absence of a structural stop matches Connors' own tested result rather than an engine limitation.

    4.2 rsi_range_reversal — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1 gates on the confirmed-ranging regime (daily trend_ranging{-1} == 1 and mixed_regime{-1} == 0), then fires LONG on rsi{-2} < 30 and rsi{-1} > 30 and SHORT on the mirror at 70, using RSI(14) on the 5m base timeframe. L2 is mean_reversion() with no take-profit/stop expression and no time-stop; the only structural piece is an explicit Layer-2 CLOSE that fires when RSI recrosses the 50 midline (rsi{-1} >= 50 long, rsi{-1} <= 50 short) — so the trade's ordinary exit is the oscillator state, while the stop/target both fall back to the campaign's tuned config. Features: RSI(14) on 5m; the daily Market State columns trend_ranging/mixed_regime (vol_baseline_window=30, stability_window=20, vol_of_vol_window=30) read as 1d higher-timeframe context.
    • Canonical source. J. Welles Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978) for RSI(14) and the 30/70 threshold recross.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Stop and target both come from the campaign's tuned ATR levels (4.0× / 3.4×) because RSI carries no intrinsic price level to convert to; the position is instead cut by the authored 50-midline CLOSE before either config level is usually reached. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based off the tuned stop distance.
    • Possible improvement. The midline recross already gives a fast, evidence-informed exit — Connors' RSI(2) research and general mean-reversion practice both indicate a nearer-mean exit outperforms holding to the far extreme for short-horizon reversion — so no change is needed on speed grounds alone.
    • Compromise. Wilder's own 30/70 framing and the classic symmetric reversal-trade convention (buy the oversold recross, exit/sell on the opposite overbought recross) define the canonical exit as the recross of the OPPOSITE extreme, not the 50 midline. The approved decision for canonical fidelity is to switch the CLOSE rule to the opposite-extreme recross at RSI 70/30 (long exit on rsi{-2} < 70 and rsi{-1} > 70, short exit on rsi{-2} > 30 and rsi{-1} < 30) — a change to the existing expression, not a new feature, trading a faster mid-range exit for one that matches Wilder's own definition literally. Not yet applied.

    4.3 stochastic_reversal — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on ranging_gate and stoch.k{-2} < 20 and cross_up(stoch.k{-2:-1}, stoch.d{-2:-1}); SHORT mirrors it at 80 with cross_down. Stochastic uses k_period=14, d_period=3 (defaults) on 5m. L2 is mean_reversion() with an explicit CLOSE on the opposite %K/%D crossover: long exits on cross_down(stoch.k{-2:-1}, stoch.d{-2:-1}), short on cross_up. No take-profit/stop expression, no time-stop — both fall back to the tuned config. Features: stochastic(14, 3) on 5m; the daily trend_ranging/mixed_regime Market State columns as 1d context.
    • Canonical source. George Lane's stochastic oscillator (Investors Intelligence, late 1950s) — entry on a %K/%D crossover out of the extreme zone, exit on the opposite crossover.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Stop and target both come from the campaign's tuned ATR levels (4.0× / 3.4×) since Stochastic carries no price level either; the opposite-crossover CLOSE is the trade's real exit. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based.
    • Possible improvement. None — every source checked is unanimous on the opposite-crossover exit as canonical, and it is already implemented exactly.
    • Compromise. None identified; this is the one oscillator in the family whose shipped exit needs no reconciliation with its named source.

    4.4 williams_reversal — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on ranging_gate and willr{-2} < -90 and willr{-1} > -80; SHORT mirrors it at -10/-20. Williams %R(14) on 5m. L2 is mean_reversion() with an explicit CLOSE on the -50 midline recross (willr{-1} > -50 long, willr{-1} < -50 short). No take-profit/stop expression, no time-stop — both fall back to the tuned config. Features: willr(14) on 5m; the daily trend_ranging/mixed_regime columns as 1d context.
    • Canonical source. Larry Williams' %R, as documented on StockCharts ChartSchool: a move back above/below -50 is explicitly named there as confirmation that an overbought/oversold reading has resolved.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Stop and target both come from the campaign's tuned ATR levels (4.0× / 3.4×) since %R carries no price level; the -50 CLOSE is the trade's real exit. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based.
    • Possible improvement. None — this is the one indicator among the family's oscillators where the -50 midline is itself the primary source's explicitly documented convention (as opposed to a secondary/derived one), so the shipped exit already matches the canon directly.
    • Compromise. None identified.

    4.5 bollinger_touch_reentry — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on ranging_gate and close{-2} < bb.lower{-2} and close{-1} > bb.lower{-1}; SHORT mirrors it on bb.upper. Bollinger period=20, std_dev=2.0 (defaults) on 5m. L2 is mean_reversion() with a structural take-profit at the middle band on both sides (bb.middle{-1}) and a 30-bar time-stop; no structural stop, so it falls back to the tuned config. Features: bollinger(20, 2.0) and close on 5m; the daily trend_ranging/mixed_regime columns as 1d context.
    • Canonical source. John Bollinger, Bollinger on Bollinger Bands — a band touch/re-entry runs until price returns to the middle band (the 20-period basis).
    • Chosen configuration and why. The take-profit is structural (bb.middle), overriding the campaign's tuned 3.4× ATR target, because Bollinger's own framing targets the basis line directly. No structural stop — Bollinger's own definition carries none — so the stop falls back to the campaign's tuned 4.0× ATR. The 30-bar time-stop is sized at ~1.5× the 20-bar band period rather than a flat constant. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based off the tuned stop distance.
    • Possible improvement. None — already faithful to the canon.
    • Compromise. None identified.

    4.6 bollinger_percent_b_snapback — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on %b{-2} < 0 and %b{-1} > 0 and zscore(close, 20) < -1.5; SHORT mirrors it (%b{-2} > 1 and %b{-1} < 1 and zscore > 1.5). No ranging_gate — the entry is regime-agnostic, since the %B band-edge cross plus the z-score stretch already select a statistically extreme move. Bollinger period=20, std_dev=2.0. L2 is mean_reversion() with a structural take-profit at the middle band on both sides (bb.middle{-1}) and a 30-bar time-stop; no structural stop. Features: bollinger(20, 2.0) and close on 5m only; the rolling z-score is computed inline via the DSL avg/std window functions over a 20-bar window, not a stored feature.
    • Canonical source. Bollinger %B (John Bollinger's normalized read of the same bands, StockCharts' treatment) — the same reversion-to-basis premise as bollinger_touch_reentry, confirmed here by a z-score stretch filter.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The take-profit is structural (bb.middle), overriding the campaign's tuned 3.4× ATR target, matching the same basis-reversion premise. No structural stop, so it falls back to the tuned 4.0× ATR. The 30-bar time-stop is sized to the same 20-bar band/z-score window bollinger_touch_reentry uses. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based.
    • Possible improvement. None — already faithful; the z-score stretch confirmation already gives the entry a statistically extreme trigger, so the expected reversion is faster than the band's own lookback, which the 30-bar stall cut already accommodates.
    • Compromise. None identified.

    4.7 zscore_reversion_to_mean — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1 computes z_now = zscore(close, 50, at=-1) and z_prev = zscore(close, 50, at=-2), then fires LONG on ranging_gate and z_now < -2 and z_now > z_prev (an extreme stretch that has started turning back toward the mean); SHORT mirrors it (z_now > 2 and z_now < z_prev). L2 is mean_reversion() with a structural take-profit at the rolling mean on both sides (avg(close{-50:-1})), a structural stop at the 3-sigma extension (avg(close{-50:-1}) ∓ 3·std(close{-50:-1})), and a 50-bar time-stop. Features: close on 5m (the z-score is a DSL avg/std computation over a 50-bar window); the daily trend_ranging/mixed_regime columns as 1d context.
    • Canonical source. Ernest Chan, Quantitative Trading / Algorithmic Trading — a mean-reverting (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-style) series reverts to its rolling mean (z→0); Chan's own guidance frames a several-sigma extension stop as one that should rarely trigger.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Both take-profit and stop are structural, overriding the campaign's tuned 3.4× / 4.0× ATR levels, because the strategy already computes the rolling mean and its dispersion directly. Trailing stays at the campaign default — structural levels do not disable it in mean_reversion(). The 50-bar time-stop is tied directly to the same 50-bar window the z-score itself reads. Slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based off the 3-sigma stop distance.
    • Possible improvement. Chan's own framework times the exit by the estimated half-life of mean reversion (ln(2)/theta, from an AR(1)/OU regression of price changes on levels over the lookback), closing a position that has not reverted after 3-4 half-lives — a time budget that adapts to each symbol's actual reversion speed, rather than a fixed 50-bar count.
    • Compromise. The half-life estimator is a new feature (an OU-process regression column), not a rule expressible today with the existing DSL primitives; until it exists, tying the time-stop to the 50-bar z-score window itself is the closest available proxy. This is a build gap, not a hard limit.

    4.8 keltner_channel_fade — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on ranging_gate and close{-2} < kc.lower{-2} and close{-1} > kc.lower{-1}; SHORT mirrors it on kc.upper. Keltner period=20, atr_period=10, multiplier=2.0 (defaults). L2 is mean_reversion() with a structural take-profit at the channel's middle line on both sides (kc.middle{-1}) and a 30-bar time-stop; no structural stop. Features: keltner(20, 10, 2.0) and close on 5m; the daily trend_ranging/mixed_regime columns as 1d context.
    • Canonical source. Chester Keltner's original channel, refined by Linda Raschke's ATR-based version (StockCharts) — fade only in a confirmed range, and hold until price reaches the channel's middle EMA line.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The take-profit is structural (kc.middle), overriding the campaign's tuned 3.4× ATR target, since the middle EMA line is the canonical reversion target. No structural stop, so it falls back to the campaign's tuned 4.0× ATR. The 30-bar time-stop is sized at ~1.5× the channel's own 20-period EMA. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based.
    • Possible improvement. None — already faithful to the canon.
    • Compromise. None identified.

    4.9 cci_extreme_reversal — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on ranging_gate and cci{-2} < -100 and cci{-1} > -100; SHORT mirrors it on +100. CCI(20) on 5m. L2 is mean_reversion() with an explicit CLOSE on CCI recrossing the 0 centerline (cci{-1} >= 0 long, cci{-1} <= 0 short). No take-profit/stop expression, no time-stop — both fall back to the tuned config. Features: cci(20) on 5m; the daily trend_ranging/mixed_regime columns as 1d context.
    • Canonical source. Donald Lambert's Commodity Channel Index (1980).
    • Chosen configuration and why. Stop and target both come from the campaign's tuned ATR levels (4.0× / 3.4×) since CCI carries no price level; the 0-centerline CLOSE is the trade's real exit. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based.
    • Possible improvement. None beyond the recross-fidelity point below.
    • Compromise. Lambert's original CCI system is trend-following, not mean-reversion: buy on a cross above +100, exit on the recross back through the SAME +100 threshold (mirrored at -100 for shorts). This strategy's entry is already a modern contrarian repurposing of CCI — fading the -100 recross rather than following it — and the 0-centerline exit is a legitimate, sourced practitioner convention for that fade specifically, but it is not Lambert's own recross rule, and StockCharts warns the plain zero-line cross alone can produce many whipsaws. The approved decision for canonical fidelity is to switch the CLOSE rule to the opposite-extreme recross (cci{-2} < 100 and cci{-1} > 100 for a long exit, cci{-2} > -100 and cci{-1} < -100 for a short exit) — a change to the existing expression, not a new feature. Not yet applied.

    4.10 mfi_exhaustion_reversal — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on ranging_gate and mfi{-2} < 20 and mfi{-1} > 20; SHORT mirrors it at 80. MFI(14) on 5m (high/low/close/volume_base inputs). L2 is mean_reversion() with an explicit CLOSE on MFI recrossing the 50 midline (mfi{-1} >= 50 long, mfi{-1} <= 50 short). No take-profit/stop expression, no time-stop — both fall back to the tuned config. Features: mfi(14) on 5m; the daily trend_ranging/mixed_regime columns as 1d context.
    • Canonical source. Gene Quong and Avrum Soudack's Money Flow Index.
    • Chosen configuration and why. Stop and target both come from the campaign's tuned ATR levels (4.0× / 3.4×) since MFI carries no price level; the 50-midline CLOSE is the trade's real exit. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based.
    • Possible improvement. None beyond the recross-fidelity point below.
    • Compromise. Quong & Soudack's own named MFI signals are the extreme thresholds (80/20, or their stricter 90/10 "truly" overbought/oversold read), divergence, and failure swings — none of them is a midline cross, and StockCharts' MFI reference explicitly cautions that "using the centerline to identify a bullish or bearish bias isn't ideal." The approved decision for canonical fidelity is to switch the CLOSE rule to the opposite-extreme recross at the stricter 90/10 level (mfi{-2} < 90 and mfi{-1} > 90 for a long exit, mfi{-2} > 10 and mfi{-1} < 10 for a short exit) — a change to the existing expression, not a new feature. Not yet applied.

    4.11 consecutive_bar_exhaustion — profile FR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on count(close{-5:-1} < open{-5:-1}) >= 4 and close{-1} < kc.lower{-1} and close{-1} > open{-1} — at least 4 of the last 5 bars closed down into a Keltner-channel extreme, with the latest bar itself turning back up (closing above its own open); SHORT mirrors it on up-bars into kc.upper with the latest bar closing below its own open. Keltner period=20/atr_period=10/multiplier=2.0. L2 is failure_reversal(): a structural take-profit at the 5-bar average on both sides (avg(close{-5:-1})), the profile's default 50% partial at +1R (the +2R runner is dropped since a structural take-profit is set), and an 8-bar time-stop. No structural stop, so it falls back to the tuned config. Features: keltner(20, 10, 2.0), close and open on 5m.
    • Canonical source. Larry Connors' multiple-days-up/-down plus reversal-bar exhaustion setups (High Probability ETF Trading, also the basis for the TPS system with Cesar Alvarez); the catalog's reversal_bar confirmation is approximated here by requiring the latest bar itself to turn back.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The take-profit is structural (avg(close{-5:-1})), overriding the campaign's tuned 3.4× ATR target, matching Connors' own moving-average-recross exit. No structural stop — Connors runs this family with none — so the stop falls back to the campaign's tuned 4.0× ATR. The 50%-at-+1R partial and 8-bar time-stop come from failure_reversal()'s fast-cut design, with the 8-bar count sized close to (roughly 1.5-2×) the entry's own 5-bar run-length window rather than a disconnected constant. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based.
    • Possible improvement. None — this is the best-aligned strategy in the family relative to its canon.
    • Compromise. The catalog's reversal_bar confirmation (a dedicated candlestick pattern) is approximated by the simpler "closed back through its own open" turn. That is a legitimate mechanical proxy, not a hard limit, but it is not a literal rendering of whichever specific reversal-bar pattern the source names.
    • Defect — wrong feature timeframe (to fix). Connors' exhaustion is ≥4 of the last 5 days closing against the trend; here count(close{-5:-1} < open{-5:-1}) >= 4 counts 5 five-minute bars (~25 min), so the multi-day-run premise is lost. Base stays 5m; the fix is to count down/up bars over 5 daily bars on a 1d bucket forward-filled to 5m (needs a daily rolling directional-bar-count feature). Feature-timeframe bug; not flagged before this audit.

    4.12 distance_from_ema_reversion — profile MR

    • Implementation. L1 computes distance_now = pct_distance(close, ema20, at=-1) and distance_prev = pct_distance(close, ema20, at=-2), then fires LONG on ranging_gate and distance_now < -0.01 and distance_now > distance_prev (price stretched more than 1% below the 20-EMA and the gap already narrowing); SHORT mirrors it (> 0.01, gap narrowing from above). L2 is mean_reversion() with a structural take-profit at the reference EMA on both sides (ema{-1}), a structural stop at 1.5× the current ATR beyond price (market_current_price{-1} ∓ 1.5 * market_atr{-1}), and a 30-bar time-stop. The stop reads the engine's built-in market_current_price/market_atr context variables rather than a features.atr() call. Features: ema(20) and close on 5m; the daily trend_ranging/mixed_regime columns as 1d context.
    • Canonical source. Moving-average-envelope / percent-distance-from-EMA mean reversion — the standard treatment behind percent-band systems, which hold from the stretch turning back until price reaches the reference moving average.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The take-profit is structural (ema{-1}), overriding the campaign's tuned 3.4× ATR target. The stop is also structural, at 1.5× market_atr beyond current price, overriding the campaign's tuned 4.0× ATR — a deliberate volatility-relative stop rather than the tuned default, since the trade's own invalidation (the stretch failing to revert) is naturally measured in ATR terms. The 30-bar time-stop is sized at ~1.5× the 20-bar EMA period. Trailing is the campaign default; slippage is the campaign's 5 bp; sizing is risk-based off the 1.5× ATR stop distance.
    • Possible improvement. Widen the stop to 2-3× ATR, matching the two best-documented ATR-multiple conventions in the literature — Van Tharp's volatility-stop teaching (2-3× ATR) and Chuck LeBeau's Chandelier Exit (3× ATR below the trade's peak, popularized via Alexander Elder's Come Into My Trading Room) — both wider than the current 1.5×.
    • Compromise. The 1.5× ATR multiple is not traceable to any named canonical source for this family; no source found prescribes 1.5× specifically, and the two best-documented ATR conventions both run wider (2-3×). A more strategy-native alternative would place the stop beyond a wider percentage envelope band, consistent with the entry's own %-distance-from-EMA units, rather than switching to ATR units at all. Neither adjustment is a hard engine limit — both are a parameter/authoring choice — but as shipped this stop's multiple is an invented convention rather than a sourced one.

    5. Volatility / structure family

    5.1 failed_breakout_reversal — profile FR

    • Implementation. L1: LONG fires on close{-2} < lowest(low{-20:-3}) and close{-1} > lowest(low{-20:-3}) and close{-1} > open{-1} — a close beyond the 20-bar low followed by a close back inside on a bullish bar; SHORT is the mirror on the 20-bar high with a bearish confirmation bar. L2 profile failure_reversal(): long_stop_expr=lowest(low{-2:-1}) / short_stop_expr=highest(high{-2:-1}) place the stop just beyond the failure wick (the breakout bar plus the confirmation bar); long_close_expr/short_close_expr add a floating CLOSE at the range midpoint, close{-1} >= (highest(high{-20:-3}) + lowest(low{-20:-3})) / 2 (mirrored <= for the short); time_stop_bars=3 cuts a stall before it reaches +0R. No take-profit expression is passed, so the profile's own +1R/50% partial and its +2R runner (_modify_tp, triggered once profit passes +1.5R) apply on top of the midpoint exit. Structural levels: stop and CLOSE are both structural; no structural take-profit. Features: BTCUSDT 5m, raw OHLCV only (high/low/close/open), a 20-bar back window (offsets -20:-3).
    • Canonical source. Connors & Raschke's "Turtle Soup" failed 20-bar-breakout fade (Street Smarts, 1995): a close beyond the 20-bar extreme that closes back inside is the Turtle Soup entry almost verbatim.
    • Chosen configuration and why. The stop is fully structural on both sides, so it overrides the campaign's tuned stop_loss_config (4x ATR) with the tighter failure-wick level the setup itself defines. Take-profit is not structural, so the campaign's take_profit_config (3.4x ATR) sets the initial target, extended toward the runner once price clears +1.5R. Trailing stays on the campaign's trailing_stop_config (ATR-based, activated at +3R, 5x ATR distance) since the profile does not opt into its own wide trail. Slippage is 5 bp; sizing is risk-based off the structural stop distance. The 3-bar time-stop and the range-midpoint floating CLOSE are both sized to Raschke's own guidance — a fast countertrend scalp closed 2-3 bars after entry, or exited on a floating target back toward the range — rather than a flat constant unrelated to the 20-bar setup.
    • Possible improvement. Raschke's Turtle Soup is explicitly a scalp with no runner: she closes the position within a few bars or on the floating target, never lets it ride toward a second, larger R-multiple. The strategy's residual +2R _modify_tp runner (and the 3.4x-ATR config target that precedes it) has no basis in that design; dropping the runner extension so the trade exits purely on its structural stop, the range-midpoint CLOSE, or the 3-bar time-stop would match the canonical scalp exactly.
    • Compromise. Not a hard limit — the runner extension is a shared piece of the failure_reversal() profile (built for reuse across other FR-family strategies that do want a runner), so trimming it here is a one-strategy parameter change, not an engine gap.
    • Defect — wrong feature timeframe (to fix). Connors & Raschke's Turtle Soup fades a failed 20-day breakout; here the 20-bar channel (-20:-3) runs on the 5m base (~1.7h) and the 3-bar stall-cut is ~15 min, compressing a multi-day scalp into ~2h. Base stays 5m; the fix is to compute the 20-bar high/low channel on a 1d bucket forward-filled to 5m (the daily channel feature shared with donchian_breakout).

    5.2 inside_bar_expansion — profile BO

    • Implementation. L1: an inside bar at -2 (high{-2} < high{-3} and low{-2} > low{-3}) followed by LONG on close{-1} > high{-2} or SHORT on close{-1} < low{-2} — a break of the inside bar's own range. L2 breakout(): long_stop_expr=low{-3} / short_stop_expr=high{-3} place the stop beyond the opposite side of the mother bar (bar -3). No take-profit expression, no CLOSE expression, and no_follow_bars is not passed, so breakout()'s default (None) applies — no time-stop exists on this strategy. The 50% partial at +1.5R (the profile default) is the only other management piece. Features: BTCUSDT 5m, raw OHLCV high/low/close only, no indicators.
    • Canonical source. Toby Crabel's narrow-range/inside-day breakout pattern (Day Trading with Short-Term Price Patterns and Opening Range Breakout, 1990).
    • Chosen configuration and why. The stop is structural on both sides (the mother-bar extreme), overriding the campaign's 4x-ATR stop_loss_config. Take-profit is not structural, so the campaign's 3.4x-ATR take_profit_config governs, alongside the campaign's ATR trailing stop (activated at +3R, 5x ATR distance). Slippage is 5 bp; sizing is risk-based off the mother-bar stop distance. No time-stop is authored, consistent with Crabel's own pattern having no bar-count exit rule beyond the intraday context it was designed for.
    • Possible improvement. Crabel's day-trading design implies the failure mode is re-entry into the compressed mother-bar range, not the clock. Adding an explicit structural CLOSE for that re-entry — close{-1} back between low{-3} and high{-3} — would give the strategy a genuine structural invalidation rule instead of relying solely on the initial stop and the campaign's generic exits.
    • Compromise. No hard limit — the mother-bar re-entry CLOSE is expressible today with the same price columns already read by the entry rule; it is simply not yet authored into action_rules.
    • Defect — wrong feature timeframe (to fix). Crabel's pattern is an inside day nested inside the prior day's range; here the inside-bar test runs on 5m bars (a 5-minute mother bar). Base stays 5m; the fix is to detect the inside-bar pattern on daily bars via a 1d bucket forward-filled to 5m (needs a daily inside-bar/mother-bar feature).

    5.3 atr_expansion_breakout — profile BO

    • Implementation. L1: atr_surge = atr{-1} > 1.3 * avg(atr{-20:-2}); LONG atr_surge and close{-1} > highest(high{-10:-2}); SHORT mirrored on the 10-bar low. L2 breakout(): long_stop_expr=lowest(low{-10:-2}) / short_stop_expr=highest(high{-10:-2}) set the stop at the opposite side of the broken 10-bar channel; long_close_expr=close{-1} < lowest(low{-5:-2}) / short_close_expr=close{-1} > highest(high{-5:-2}) add a shorter, half-width opposite-channel exit — a Turtle-style asymmetric channel. No take-profit expression, no no_follow_bars. Features: BTCUSDT 5m, ATR(14), raw OHLCV high/low/close.
